newsitem.title: UK: EMU poses thorny problems for bond futures -LIFFE.
newsitem.headline: EMU poses thorny problems for bond futures -LIFFE.

text.p: Europe's biggest derivatives exchange, LIFFE, is grappling with the difficult problem of designing bond futures that will operate under European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), an exchange executive said.
The London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE) has to decide what cash bonds will form the basis for its futures contracts when EMU begins in 1999.

"It's extremely difficult for an exchange like us," Guiliano Gregorio, a director of business development at LIFFE told Reuters in an interview. "What bond will be delivered against the futures contract?" he said.

LIFFE has already made provisions in Euromark and short sterling interest rate contracts for the euro. Settlement will be determined by reference to British Bankers Association settlement rates for three-month deposits of euro or other such London interbank rates.
But developing a futures contract on a 10-year bond will be more difficult, said Gregorio, who is in charge of interest rate products.
The main issue is whether to create individual futures contracts on individual cash bonds such as the German euro bond or to create one large futures contract that will incorporate all euro bonds.

"On one side we just have to change the currency," said Gregorio. "On the other side it will be a very big futures contract on a homogeneous government contract, or any scenario between these two," he said.
Designing one euro bond future would be tricky because different euro bonds could have different credit risks and hence different values, Gregorio said.

Problems would also arise from players using the "cheapest to deliver" underlying bond, he added. For instance any one of several cash gilts in a pool can be delivered onto the LIFFE gilt future and players usually opt for the cheapest.
But under a euro bond this would always be the weakest bond in the system -- the Italian euro for example.
"If you are a holder of German government bonds and you want to hedge your position, you don't want to use something that is tracking Italian government bonds," said Gregorio.

One idea would be to have the future contract settled in cash as is done currently in interest rate futures and have that determined by an average of rates for cash bonds denominated in euros from different countries.
But here too difficulties arise, Gregorio said.
"For bond markets that's not thought to be very efficient because the most important thing is to have convergence between the cash markets and futures market," he said.
"The best way to ensure this convergence takes place is through forced delivery," he said. "This also gives arbitrageurs a possibility to eliminate all the discrepancies in the two markets."
A banker in London agreed cash settlement would rob the market of a large group of participants who play the market for arbitrage opportunities in deliverable bonds.
Gregorio said a group of experts at LIFFE have already begun thrashing out various solutions but they still have a little time.

While 1999 interest rate future contracts had to be listed by March this year -- hence the urgency for the euro provisos for those products -- bond futures that mature post-EMU do not have to be listed until June 1998, he said.

But LIFFE faces challenges from outside as well. Germany's DTB exchange, which also has a Bund futures contract and Paris's MATIF, which lists French bond futures, are also hustling to be the centre of trade in what some analysts expect to be a smaller debt market after EMU.
